plan.chapterName: OpenStax Precalculus 2e, chapter 3: Polynomial and Rational Functions
plan.contextChunk: This figure graphs a rational function on a coordinate plane and marks the two distinct ways its graph breaks. The horizontal axis is labeled x and ticked at odd values from -3 through 9; the vertical axis is ticked at even values from -6 to 6 over a dotted gray grid. The teal curve comes in two branches. The left branch enters from the far left almost flat and just above the x-axis, carries a small hollow open circle at x equal to -1 marking a point removed from the graph, then descends through the x-axis at x equal to 1 and drops steeply, running off the bottom of the frame as it approaches x equal to 3. The right branch begins high just to the right of x equal to 3, falls quickly, then levels off toward the right edge near y equal to 1. A red dashed vertical line stands at x equal to 3, labeled below the axis in red as Vertical asymptote at x = 3. A blue annotation at the upper left reads Removable discontinuity at x = -1, with a thin arrow to the open circle. Setting the hollow dot against the dashed line is the contrast being drawn: one break is a single missing point, the other sends the curve toward infinity on both sides.

interactionPlan.concept: A rational function can break in two fundamentally different ways: a removable discontinuity, where a single point is missing from an otherwise smooth curve, and a vertical asymptote, where the function grows without bound on both sides.
elements: Coordinate plane with dotted gray grid spanning x from about -4 to 10 and y from -7 to 7
Horizontal x-axis with arrowhead and label 'x', tick labels at -3, -1, 1, 3, 5, 7, 9
Vertical y-axis with arrowhead and label 'y', tick labels at -6, -4, -2, 2, 4, 6
Teal left branch: enters from far left nearly flat just above the x-axis, crosses the x-axis at x = 1, then plunges steeply downward off the bottom of the frame as x approaches 3
Small hollow open circle (teal outline, white fill) on the left branch at x = -1 marking the removed point
Teal right branch: descends from high above near x just greater than 3, falls steeply, then levels off approaching y = 1 at the right edge
Red dashed vertical line at x = 3 spanning the full plot height
Red label below the axis: 'Vertical asymptote at x = 3'
Blue annotation at upper left: 'Removable discontinuity at x = -1' with a thin arrow pointing to the open circle
Movable trace point marker on the curve with a readout of (x, y)
Optional dashed horizontal line at y = 1 indicating the end behavior of the right branch
Formula caption showing the function in factored and cancelled forms

interactions.teaches: That the hole and the dashed line are two different kinds of failure: one removes a single point, the other destroys the function's values near a whole line.
interactions.label: Highlight break

interactions.teaches: That approaching x = 3 from either side drives the function value to negative or positive infinity, so no single value can patch the break.
interactions.label: Trace point at x =

interactions.teaches: That the hole comes from a factor that cancels in the algebra — the simplified function is perfectly smooth at x = -1, and only the original's domain excludes that one point.
interactions.label: Algebraic form

demo_steps.title: The whole graph
demo_steps.narration: A single rational function drawn in two teal branches. Two things interrupt it: a tiny hollow circle at x = -1 and a red dashed line at x = 3.

demo_steps.title: A single missing point
demo_steps.narration: Highlighting the removable discontinuity shows the curve arriving at x = -1 from both sides at the same height — only the one point is punched out.

demo_steps.title: Why it is removable
demo_steps.narration: Cancelling the shared (x + 1) factor gives a function that is perfectly continuous there. Redefining one value would repair the graph entirely.

demo_steps.title: Approaching x = 3 from the left
demo_steps.narration: Now drag the trace point toward 3 from the left. The y-value dives past -6 and keeps falling — there is no height to land on.

demo_steps.title: Approaching x = 3 from the right
demo_steps.narration: From the right the value rockets upward instead. Opposite infinities on the two sides mean this break can never be patched by a single point.

demo_steps.title: Two breaks, two causes
demo_steps.narration: The hole comes from a factor that cancels; the asymptote comes from a factor that survives in the denominator. Same graph, two very different failures.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: A denominator factor that cancels leaves only a hole you could fill with one value; a factor that does not cancel sends the function to infinity, and no single value can ever repair it.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Textbook-style coordinate plane on white with a light dotted gray grid, axes in black with arrowheads and italic x and y labels; odd-numbered ticks on x (-3 to 9), even-numbered ticks on y (-6 to 6). The function curve is drawn in a medium teal, fairly thick, in two branches: the left branch comes in from the far left just above y = 0, stays nearly flat, crosses the x-axis at x = 1, then bends sharply downward and exits the bottom of the frame just left of x = 3; the right branch enters the top of the frame just right of x = 3, drops steeply, and flattens toward y = 1 by x = 9. A white-filled teal-outlined open circle sits on the left branch at x = -1. A bold red dashed vertical line sits at x = 3 with the red caption 'Vertical asymptote at x = 3' placed below the x-axis to the right. A blue multi-line annotation 'Removable discontinuity at x = -1' sits in the upper-left margin with a thin black arrow to the open circle. When a break is highlighted, that marker brightens and thickens while the other dims to gray. The trace point is a filled dot on the curve with a small coordinate readout that turns red and reads large magnitudes as x nears 3. In the cancelled view, show the simplified formula and a faint ghost of the filled-in point at x = -1 while keeping the open circle visible.

plan.authoredInteractions:
- Toggle between removable discontinuity and vertical asymptote; the learner switches the highlighted break, the open circle or dashed vertical line brightens, and the contrast between a missing point and unbounded behavior becomes clear.
- Slider for x approaching 3; the learner moves a trace point toward the vertical asymptote from either side, the y-value shoots downward or upward, and it becomes clear why x = 3 is not a removable hole.
- Toggle factor-cancelled view: the learner reveals the cancelled factor that fixes the removable discontinuity at x = -1, keeping the hole in place while showing that only one function value is missing from an otherwise continuous branch.

authoredContext:
Notice that x+1 is a common factor to the numerator and the denominator. The zero of this factor, x=−1, is the location of the removable discontinuity. Notice also that x–3 is not a factor in both the numerator and denominator. The zero of this factor, x=3, is the vertical asymptote. See the figure.

Graph of f(x)=(x^2-1)/(x^2-2x-3) with its vertical asymptote at x=3 and a removable discontinuity at x=-1.

discrepancies: The two near-asymptote branches are sampled out to |y| ≈ 8.7, so they run well past the dotted grid (down to the very bottom edge of the canvas and above the y-axis arrow tip); in the source both tips stop just past y = ±6 inside the grid field, giving a more compact composition.

The x-tick label '3' is dropped to a second, lower row to dodge the red dashed line, so it reads as a floating '3' detached from the tick row instead of sitting in line with −3, −1, 1, 5, 7, 9 as in the source.

Grid field density/extent differs slightly: the source dotted rectangle is clearly bounded around x ∈ [−3.5, 9.5], y ∈ [−6.5, 6.5] and reads as a uniform dot field, while the generated dots are fainter/sparser and partly overwhelmed by the curve overshoot.

The blue caption's leader arrow starts from the middle of the text block and is fairly long/shallow; in the source it is a short steep arrow from just under 'at x = −1' to the open circle, so the pointer relationship is tighter.
The right-hand branch in the generated figure flattens slightly lower/closer to y = 1 than the source's visually higher approach (~y = 1.3–1.5 near x = 9), a small trend/scale difference.
evaluation.notes: A faithful, well-composed reproduction of the rational-function figure with correct hole/asymptote math and a rich, genuinely pedagogical set of interactions (6-step player, break-type toggle, trace slider, factored/cancelled form); the main weaknesses are branch tips overshooting the dotted grid to the canvas edge and the '3' tick label displaced to its own row.
action_items: Clamp the near-asymptote branch sampling to about |y| ≤ 6.6 so the teal arrowheads terminate just inside the dotted grid, as in the source, instead of running to the canvas edges.
Keep the '3' tick label in the same baseline row as the other x-tick labels; move it a few pixels to the right of the dashed line (or add a white halo) rather than dropping it a row.
Shorten and steepen the blue leader arrow so it emanates from just below 'at x = −1' and points closely at the open circle, matching the source's tight pointer.

Slightly strengthen the dotted grid (contrast/extent) and ensure it is clipped to the source's x ∈ [−3.5, 9.5], y ∈ [−6.5, 6.5] rectangle so the field boundary reads as clearly as in the printed figure.

feedback.rationale: The concept and interaction structure are correct; all action items are concrete rendering fixes (clamping curve sampling, tick label placement, leader arrow geometry, grid clipping/contrast) that belong to the generator.
